lines.text: We want the spouse caregiver to keep their own health and have someone to lean on.
The caregiver gets regular breaks
The caregiver has someone to talk to
The caregiver's own medical needs are not put off

items.quote: There is no respite from this disease which progresses far too quickly.
I knew caring for both of them would be to much.
Right now I can't remember the happy times.
I am so riddled with grief and guilt that I am almost non-functional.
I don't really have anywhere else to vent.
I cannot seem to force myself to visit with her
Now, when my help is here and I run an errand I dread going back.
I am sick and worn out
The vocalizations are like a wavering whimper. Pretty much like Chinese water torture.
I just want to be home, not seeing anyone, not accomplishing anything.
Just counting the hours until I can go to bed for another night of restless sleep.
Trying to find the balance between being a partner and a caregiver has been one of my biggest challenges in caring for my DH.
Like you, I still work and arranging care at home is difficult.
I just feel so angry and tired and unsupported all the time.
They want him to exercise, but I cannot go for walks with him due to my rollator and bad knee from an irrepairable Achille's tendon tear.
I think I am an awful person for hoping one of those things happen sooner not later.
The stress is so overwhelming for me I fear a stroke or heart attack.
Sometimes I get frustrated by the re-doing as it is more work than if I had done it in the beginning
I am exhausted, constantly crying through frustration and exhaustion.
The entertainment and engagement effort is exhausting to me.
I have so much on my plate as full time caregiver I just can’t do any more.
I am tired of doing it all - cooking, cleaning, daily laundry, paying bills, grocery shoping, doctors appointments, I’m even tired of crying everyday
I don’t want to dump on my friends or family.
pretty much everything has changed and it is non stop on my side and it drains me to know end.
I work full time and it is just me. No family around this area.
I found these conversations very confronting and for most of this time I was in tears, distraught.
It’s very hard being solely responsible for him.
I don’t know how much longer this journey will last.
I’m a fixer and I can’t fix this.

lines.text: We want caregivers to handle agitation, repeated questions and refusal without anger or exhaustion.
The caregiver finds something that calms the person when the usual tactics stop working
Evening restlessness does not end the day in conflict
The caregiver knows when to ask a doctor about behavior or medicine

items.quote: Her anxiety/ agitation/ emotional outbursts and general "altered states" are recently getting more pronounced.
As my husband's mixed dementia got worse and his behavior became more aggressive I consented when his doctor suggested more drugs.
sometimes the best caregiver behavioral techniques and environmental adjustments just aren't enough to prevent unsustainable crazytown.
My dh is not much of a talker about difficult things
I know patience is the #1 need in a caregiver, and I'm doing my best, and trying to teach our girls the same (ages 17, 15, and 12)...but we fall short way too often.
if all the necessary details aren't there (where, what time do we leave, who's driving, who's going...), then it's a major struggle.
Woke up at 3:20 with husband cussing loudly, trying to get out of bed.
How should I respond to the same question multiple times everyday.
basically all day long he is asking me where is she when will she be back how is she getting home etc.
she said it was stuff she wanted to take home, we have lived here for 30 years
At times, I actually miss the repetitive questions, as opposed to the awful silence.
I've been doing this for 10+ years for a combative husband who is in diapers.
Sometimes she gets down right mean, like sundowning on steroids'.
My husband says "no" to every question.
Can't communicate at all.
In the last week or so, DH has been trying to pick up things that are only the pattern in either the floor, bedspread, or countertop.
She is determined to stay independent and takes offense to any questions or reminders about medications and other normal daily questions or reminders.
told me I’m not a good caregiver
This changing relationship between us is so painful and frustrating.
We just cannot get along, and I can’t find reactions or lack of reactions that work with her.
I am very angry about how this has changed my life and often engage him in arguments and yell at him.
I have to be sensitive to slight changes in his mood and to my reactions to things that happen because it’s easy for me to react strongly and hurt his feelings.
I am wondering whether this is something not to bother pointing out, as this tends to provoke a range of emotions, from irritation to anger.
She needs to be doing something all the time and expects me to provide her with something to do.
my DH has low tolerance for interruptions to his routine… especially after 5 pm or so.
My wife, who has Alzheimer’s, is constantly saying she wants to go home (we are living at home), she doesn’t want to be here anymore, and she can’t do this anymore.
I’ve tried telling her she’s safe here, asking her to tell me about home, and other tactics I’ve seen here and elsewhere, to no avail.
The constant criticism, being blamed for everything…it goes on and on.

lines.text: We want bathing, toileting, medicines and eating to be manageable at home.
Night-time incontinence does not wreck the caregiver's sleep
The person takes medicine without a fight
Doctors can see the readings or notes the caregiver keeps

items.quote: He refuses to shower even with help.
DH is up and down from about 3.30pm every night, a few overshoots in the bathroom
It just got to be too much for me with the incontinence, helping her to eat, refusing showing, refusing to change her depends etc.
My husband hates being cleaned up, and yells "help me!" the entire time.
Sedative meds just make it more dangerous most times.
It’s impossible to know if she’s in distress but it doesn’t appear that she is.
Hospice is stumped because she doesn’t react to medications like most patients.
the neurologist definitely piled up way too many drugs to try to manage her aggression.
My wife has determined to not take her meds when I offer them to her.
She's put it on her dry hair before outside the bath cycle.
my spouse does not remember that she has eaten and therefore constantly eats.
She also forgets when she has a glass of wine if we go out to dinner and comes home and pours another.
We have very little room to store a big arm cuff unit
It's so hard to gauge precision from reviews.
My husband had severe fluctuations in blood pressure and the doctors found nothing to cause it.
I have trouble getting him in the car. He gained alot of weight he is 200 lbs. I have trouble dressing him and getting him in shower.
I am constantly tired because, he just got a catheter.
If I happen to fall asleep, hubby, a type 2 diabetic will sneak ice cream and anything sweet he can find.
We are on free food from local pantries, which results in a high number of carbs which we cannot do much about

theme: Safety when they are alone or out

lines.text: We want the person to be safe when the caregiver is not with them and when they go out.
The caregiver can leave the house briefly knowing the person is safe
Public places work for a couple, for example restrooms
A conversation about driving can happen in time

items.quote: I'm finding it really difficult to leave my DW to get a haircut, attend to car repairs/ maintenance, go to my own dr's & dentists appts.
I'm still worried about her safety when I'm away as well as her frantic phone calls minutes after I leave
he is NOT safe to leave alone.
Last night she tried to do something while helping to cook dinner that was a clear fire hazard
enough to make my girls not really want to ride with her.
Yet, our neurologist is insistent on me having her supervised 24/7.
My biggest concern was if he’d know what to do in an emergency.
Walking is becoming difficult because she tries to open other apartment doors.
lately he gets confused when he goes into the men’s room when we’re out somewhere.
I’ve been noticing when he drives he’s slowing down at all intersections even if the light is green.
I'm so heartbroken that this might be a conversation we need to have quickly. I thought we had time.
when there’s no family restroom and my DH has to go into the men’s room by himself and there’s no other men going on or coming out
The falls started and I can’t get him up off the floor.
he wouldn't think to call 911 if there was a fire or other emergency

lines.text: We want caregivers to trust paid help and know what happened while they were away.
The caregiver knows how an aide's visit went
A hospice or aide visit happens as promised
The caregiver can leave the person with others for a few hours

items.quote: My DW will not consent to either so that is a remaining hurdle.
then one day didn’t show up with no phone call or anything to alert us to her quitting.
I’m afraid to contact some of these as they will share my contact info to anyone they think could give them a
It’s hard for me to leave him in someone else’s care even for a few hours
The very first day, a lady showed up at 8:00am thinking she was going to give me, rather than my wife a shower.
Most days the aide comes while I am at work, and by evening I realize I honestly do not know how the visit went.
I feel guilty double-checking on people, but I feel worse not knowing.
I was worried about counting on an aide coming every day and being reliable.
when I was gone for a few hours at a time, she had nothing to hold her accountable, she didn't do anything at all.
It’s hard for me to leave him in someone else’s care even for a few hours because I know his specific needs
I couldn't survive without this help but it's not enough.
The fact that I would suggest it would upset her and wouldn’t be happy about it

lines.text: We want families to place a spouse in memory care at the right time, in a good place, and to be able to afford it.
The caregiver can judge when home care is no longer enough
The caregiver can find a good place and pay for it
Care in the new place meets the spouse's needs

items.quote: When they started leaving her in her room all day in the same dirty clothes, I found another place as quickly as I could.
I took my DH to memory care a few months ago as I could no longer take care of him at home.
the staff mostly did just enough to "get by" until I pressed them on things.
The adjustment for me is tougher than I thought.
Don't know how we would afford to go to assisted living and if they even have units were we could be together.
Honestly, there is no chance we will be able to pay for any memory care.
It is a huge decision for us, as what will I have after he’s gone? And living on my income if/when he is in MC will be tight!
the weekend staffing level is not as good as the weekdays. I have to visit him most days to make sure he is ok.

lines.text: We want the spouse's money, bills and exposure to scams under control.
The caregiver can take over bills that were left behind
The person cannot be scammed or overspend
Care costs can be planned

items.quote: He has always taken care of all our finances. He refuses to give up control to me.
When DH nearly lost us $30,000 to a scammer, I realized that he wasn't always thinking clearly.
After DW wrote a check for 10K to a family member , I shut her down.
We are now living the results of DW in early stages getting scammed multiple times, turning our finances upside down.
I am terrified of not being able to keep the house.
She bought "one or two things" on TEMU the other day...12 things totaling over $200.
I am so overwhelmed with his bills- left so unintended- and the lack of addressing so many things when he walked out of his job
I’m struggling with figuring out health insurance for myself and I’m tired.
Not sure what help to apply for first.

lines.text: We want a diagnosis and treatment without long waits.
A person with new symptoms sees a specialist within weeks
The family understands what is wrong

items.quote: waiting 6 months feels like an eternity to me.
The doctor seemed reluctant to do blood work or,scan for plaques, and I’m not really sure why?
DW finally getting actual sustained treatment after nine months of insurance changes, delays, one rogue neuro PA, etc.
we had lived with growing symptoms that were putting terrible strain on us for years.
At one office, the scheduler told me they had no openings for several months.
We swere promised a doctor visit but that never happened.
There’s something off with some of his cognitive abilities but we do not have a why or what it is.

theme: Relatives and others not helping or criticizing

lines.text: We want family and friends to support the caregiver, not criticize.
The caregiver has family who step in
Criticism from relatives does not add to the stress

items.quote: those I held near and dear are “ too busy” to lend a hand, give me a call, or ask how I’m doing.
the bigger problem for me is his daughter and exwife that have given me more grief than anyone else. They aren't supportive, they degrade me
She was upset that my DH did not have a polo shirt and jeans on.
